svg.text: Divide the data into train / test (e.g. 80% / 20%)
Perform the outer k-fold on train
For each outer fold, split its train part again into
an inner k-fold (the outer val fold is set aside
the next hyperparameters to try; adaptive ones use
the average inner-CV losses so far
Collect the best hyperparameters (θ) per outer fold
(θ = the set with the lowest average inner loss)
Retrain on each outer train part with its θ
and score on its held-out val (val1/2/3)
Average the outer scores per model
Compare the averages and pick the best model
Tune the winner once more on the full training set
with ONE plain k-fold CV + optimizer (not nested) → θ*,
retrain on the full training set with θ*,
and test once on the test set
inside each fold, on its train part only.
The models fitted in steps 4–5 and 7 are thrown away;
The number to report is the final test score (step 10).
Outer scores only compare models; the winner's
Test data (used once, at the end)
Whole outer fold, reused in step 7
Outer k-fold CV (k = 3): train is split into 3 folds
Whole outer fold 1 (train1 + val1) goes to step 7 – val1 never enters the tuning
to try, from the avg losses so far
Retrain on train1 with θ1, then score on val1
Whole outer fold 2 (train2 + val2) goes to step 7 – val2 never enters the tuning
to try, from the avg losses so far
Retrain on train2 with θ2, then score on val2
Whole outer fold 3 (train3 + val3) goes to step 7 – val3 never enters the tuning
to try, from the avg losses so far
Retrain on train3 with θ3, then score on val3
One plain k-fold CV + optimizer (not nested) → θ*

Why tune again? Steps 3–9 only choose the model. θ1–θ3 were each tuned on a different subset of train, so the final θ* is tuned on all of it. This is one ordinary CV, at a similar cost to a single inner loop.
